headline: Sacred River Dolphins of Cambodia Show Signs of Recovery
meta_description: A successful breeding season brings six new calves to Cambodia's Irrawaddy dolphin population, raising hopes for recovery of one of the world's most endangered…
summary_short: Six newborn Irrawaddy dolphins born in Cambodia this season bring the endangered population to 118 individuals, signaling that recovery is possible with community protec…
body:
A successful breeding season has brought six newborn calves to Cambodia's Irrawaddy dolphin population, raising the sub-population to 118 individuals along a 75-mile section of the Mekong River in the country's northeast. These snub-nosed dolphins, believed by Laotians and Cambodians to be reincarnations of their ancestors, represent one of the most endangered cetacean populations in the world. The birth of these calves suggests that despite decades of environmental pressure from dams, fishing practices, and habitat loss, these sacred animals can still recover if threats are sufficiently controlled. Local conservationists view the calving season as concrete evidence that food sources remain adequate to support population growth.

The greatest danger facing young dolphins comes from gillnet fishing, which proves especially lethal to calves unfamiliar with avoiding boats and the sounds of fishermen. Though illegal fishing still occurs within protected areas, it reportedly happens on a limited scale. Starting in 2014, the World Wildlife Fund's Cambodia chapter launched a joint conservation program aimed at reducing the community's heavy dependence on fishing, diversifying local livelihoods instead. This approach reflects a broader conservation truth: a pioneering study found that community buy-in and local attitudes are the strongest predictors of whether an endangered species can recover.

In this case, the Irrawaddy dolphin has an advantage few endangered animals possess. The people living alongside these dolphins hold them in reverent regard, viewing them not as obstacles to their way of life but as beings deserving protection. Local residents have even been willing to risk confrontation to stop illegal fishing in protected zones. This deep cultural connection—rooted in spiritual beliefs and folklore about dolphins rescuing drowning villagers and protecting people from crocodiles—may ultimately prove as vital to these dolphins' survival as any dam removal or fishing regulation.
quick_facts: Six newborn Irrawaddy dolphins born in recent breeding season
Population now 118 dolphins in 75-mile section of Mekong River
Cambodians and Laotians believe dolphins are reincarnated ancestors
World Wildlife Fund launched joint conservation program in 2014
Gillnet fishing remains greatest threat to calves
